problems.description: Channel extraction/validation logic is duplicated in _handle_message (computed once at the top, then re-computed identically in the subscribe/unsubscribe branch), inflating cognitive complexity (+50).
Behavioral ambiguity: a 'direct' message carrying a channel field silently falls through to a channel broadcast instead of a direct send, which could misroute messages.
Channel name accepted from two places (payload and top-level message) in subscribe/unsubscribe, creating an implicit precedence rule that is easy to misuse.

strengths: Backwards-compatible broadcast signature (channel defaults to None) so existing callers are unaffected.
Consistent JSON responses via the new _json_response helper across /health, /channels, and /subscribers endpoints.
Correctly hoists the Connection: upgrade check so any path can upgrade, fixing the previous /health-only behavior.
Clean cleanup of empty channels in both _remove and unsubscribe keeps state tidy.
Tests added for channel isolation and unsubscribe behavior.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent pub/sub channel feature that fits the existing server architecture and patterns, introducing only minor maintainability debt from duplicated channel-validation logic.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +46: per-endpoint helper methods (_health_response, _channels_response, _subscribers_response) were inlined into _process_request, and _sqlite_path added a multi-branch URL parser; this regresses the prior separation of concerns.

Mixed concurrency model: sqlite3.connect() (blocking, sync) runs per call inside an asyncio event loop guarded by threading.Lock()/RLock(), risking event-loop stalls and inconsistent thread-safety semantics.
_persist and _history open a fresh SQLite connection per message/query rather than reusing a connection pool.
Docstrings removed from previously documented methods (timestamp, bound_port, _make_message, __init__), losing API self-documentation.
Convention violations in test_app.py (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE module constants) and transport.py (UPPER_CASE constants) per static analysis.
The commit widens the runtime surface (redis.asyncio, sqlite3, env-driven REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL) with no explicit failure/fallback path when Redis is unreachable.

strengths: Adds Redis pub/sub, enabling multi-instance fan-out and horizontal scaling of the notification service.
Introduces SQLite message retention with bounded pagination (limit clamped to 1000) and a /messages endpoint.
Validates query params defensively, returning 400 on malformed limit/offset instead of raising.
Zero new bugs, smells, or code duplication per SonarQube; reuses the existing _json_response helper and class structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A functional integration (Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence) that delivers the scaling goal but at the cost of significantly raised complexity (+46), degraded maintainability (inlined handlers, stripped docstrings), and a mixed sync/async threading model that burdens the event loop.

problems.description: self._server typed as Any where a concrete Server type was previously used — the seam erases static type safety at the exact boundary where the concrete transport type is known (transport.py owns the Server type now).

Partial abstraction leak: self.clients still stores websockets ServerConnection objects while all sends go through transport by client_id — the stored connections now serve only as membership markers, so the server remains coupled to websockets types despite the new abstraction.

Transport selection mixes constructor injection with ambient TRANSPORT env-var branching inside __init__, which makes the selection path hard to test and duplicates config responsibility that belongs in a factory.
Redundant configuration: port is passed both to WebSocketTransport(port) at construction and to transport.start(host, port), a duplicated-parameter smell that can drift.
Module-level constants in new transport.py should be UPPER_CASE per the measured convention violations (score 0.82).
Flagged discrepancy: two of the three measured convention violations reference test_app.py (not shown in this diff); if that file is untouched, those count as pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Extracts a clean BaseTransport ABC that decouples app.py from websockets internals and enables alternate transports (e.g., SSE/TCP) without touching core server logic.
Centralizes send/error handling in transport.broadcast with a failed-recipients return, collapsing the messy per-connection gather logic in _deliver.
Constructor injection of the transport enables test doubles without network exposure.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid transport-abstraction refactor that decouples the server from WebSocket internals and simplifies delivery logic, held back only by minor type-erasure, config-hygiene, and convention warts.

problems.description: Magic numbers for the rate window (60s) and cleanup interval (3600s) are hardcoded rather than env-driven, unlike RATE_LIMIT and MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS.
The local fallback _rate_windows dict is never pruned, so unbounded memory growth is possible under many client IDs once Redis is unavailable.
SonarQube convention score 0.82 with violations in test_app.py (PascalCase class, non-UPPER module constants) and transport.py (module constants not UPPER_CASE).

strengths: New features reuse existing idioms: _connect_db(), _json_response(), _db_lock, and the async cleanup task mirrors the established _redis_task lifecycle.
Parameterized SQL throughout, plus input validation on channel/since/limit before hitting the database.
Graceful degradation from Redis to an in-process rate limiter rather than failing hard.
The /history endpoint fits the existing message/channels endpoint surface and adds a supporting index on (channel, timestamp).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted cross-cutting session that extends the notification server with rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and per-channel history while faithfully following the app's established patterns; only minor maintainability nits (magic intervals, unpruned rate-window dict) and a 0.82 convention score (test/transport constants) hold it back.

compounding_issues: Session 3 introduced three sources of truth (in-memory clients/channels, Redis subscription sets, SQLite history) that all had to be kept in sync; sessions 4-5 worked around rather than resolved this, e.g. session 5 added a local rate-limit fallback alongside the Redis limiter instead of unifying state.

Session 1 locked in a single-file app.py monolith holding routing, persistence, rate limiting, and messaging together; only session 4 split out transport.py, and the DB/HTTP/WS logic stayed coupled in app.py through session 5.
Hand-rolled SQLite URL parsing (session 3's _sqlite_path with multiple edge cases) forced session 5 to bolt on :memory: shared-cache handling on top, growing complexity in the storage layer.
Blocking sqlite3 calls (connect/INSERT/SELECT) run directly in async handlers behind a threading lock, blocking the event loop; this pattern from session 3 was never fixed.
Session 3's Redis probe in start() made behavior environment-dependent (Redis up vs down changes delivery semantics and test outcomes), and Redis vs local delivery paths drifted apart over time.
Session 4-5 committed runtime artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc, messages.db), a hygiene regression in an otherwise clean history.
key_decisions: Session 1 discarded the Flask auth seed entirely and greenfielded an async WebSocket notification server (asyncio + websockets) with OS-assigned ports and health-over-WebSocket-hook for testability.

Session 2 fixed the wire protocol (broadcast/direct/system/subscribe/unsubscribe) and multiplexed HTTP introspection endpoints (/channels, /channels/<name>/subscribers) on the same WebSocket listener.

Session 3 added a Redis pub/sub backbone with graceful local-delivery fallback for multi-instance scaling, plus SQLite persistence and a /messages history endpoint, turning an ephemeral server into a durable one.
Session 4 extracted a BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction so messaging logic no longer depends on the WebSocket server, enabling alternative transports and cleaner unit tests.

Session 5 layered cross-cutting operational concerns: Redis-backed rate limiting with local fallback, TTL-based message retention with a background cleanup loop, and per-channel history pagination with since/limit/has_more semantics plus a DB index.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily from a clean, minimal async core in session 1 through a coherent feature layer in session 2 and a meaningful architectural jump in session 3 (Redis + SQLite durability). Session 4's transport extraction was the high point — a genuine decoupling that kept all nine tests green while restructuring internals. Session 5 broadened scope (rate limiting, TTL cleanup, paginated history) with tests growing 5→7→9→9→11 monotonically, but it added features on top of the accumulating dual-state complexity rather than paying it down, so the arc is 'improving design quality' up to session 4, then a plateau where feature breadth outpaces internal consolidation.
story_review.summary: A coherent greenfield→features→integration→refactor→cross-cutting arc that steadily added real capability and tests, peaking at the session 4 transport refactor while leaving a multi-source-of-truth state model as the story's one persistent architectural debt.
